title: Modern modules inside a GNN layer

hook.title: Good kitchen habits
hook.text: Classic GNN layers are a fine recipe, but real kitchens add good habits. **Batch norm** is *tasting for balance*: before the next step, re-centre and re-scale ingredients so no one flavour overwhelms training. **Dropout** is *benching random players in practice* so the team can't lean on a few stars; on match day everyone plays. And the **activation** is the oven setting: ReLU for most dishes, sigmoid only when the output must stay in a narrow range.
hook.recall: Remember the kitchen habits: batch norm balances (zero mean, unit variance), dropout benches players only during practice (training), and activations set the non-linearity: ReLU by default.

tasks: Batch norm: change shift and scale. What are the mean and variance afterwards?
Dropout: compare training vs testing. How many neurons are active in each?
explore.takeaway: Batch norm: re-centre to zero mean, re-scale to unit variance (stabilises training). Dropout: zero neurons with probability $p$ in training, use all at test (prevents overfitting). ReLU is the most commonly used activation.

build.template: Batch norm re-centres to {0} mean and re-scales to {1} variance. Dropout turns neurons off during {2} and uses all neurons at {3}.

questions.prompt: The goal of batch normalisation in a GNN layer is to:
options: Prevent overfitting by turning neurons off
Control the importance of a message
questions.explanation: Re-centre to zero mean and re-scale to unit variance: tasting for balance. (Dropout prevents overfitting; attention/gating controls message importance.)

questions.prompt: A batch of one feature across three nodes is $[2,4,6]$. Batch-normalise the **first** value (subtract the mean, divide by the standard deviation; ignore $\epsilon$). 3 decimals.

options: Batch norm re-centres embeddings to zero mean
Dropout regularises a network to prevent overfitting
In a GNN, dropout is applied to the linear layer in the message function $m_u^{(l)}=W^{(l)}h_u^{(l-1)}$
At test time dropout randomly switches off neurons
questions.explanation: Randomly benching players is a practice-time habit only.

questions.prompt: When should you use a sigmoid activation according to the slides?
options: Only when you want to restrict the range of your embeddings
questions.explanation: ReLU is the most commonly used; sigmoid $\sigma(x_i)=1/(1+e^{-x_i})$ only for range restriction.

questions.prompt: *“If I train with dropout $p=0.5$, then at test time I must also randomly drop half the neurons to match.”* What’s wrong?
options: At test time we use all neurons for the computation
Dropout can’t be used at train time
Test time doesn’t use any neurons
questions.explanation: Slide 8: during testing, use all the neurons.
